items.text:
Welcome to the Eater Heatmap, focusing on the hottest new openings in Brooklyn this month.

Eater editors do thorough reporting on the most exciting restaurant openings to hit their city, as well as smaller openings worth having on the radar. In this map, we narrow the field to those places in Brooklyn that are drawing the most excitement, buzz, crowds, and early positive chatter, focusing largely on restaurants that have only been open for six months or less. When an Eater editor has already been to a place, we share insider tips on what to expect and what’s worth ordering as well.

New to the list in October: A Top Chef alum’s new Tamil and South Indian restaurant Mythily in Williamsburg; revived Cobble Hill Italian restaurant Sam’s; and 148 Noble Street, the new Greenpoint restaurant with NOLA leanings. For now, we’ve removed Arthur, Lalaon, and Titan.

For more New York dining recommendations, check out the new hotspots in Manhattan and Queens. And for an insider’s perspective on how to eat well no matter where you are in NYC, pick up our book: The Eater Guide to New York City.

Former Chez Ma Tante chef de cuisine Gabriel Borges and Five Leaves alum Eric Carney stuck to their Greenpoint neighborhood with 148 Noble Street, named helpfully for its address, in September. Borges is offering a seasonal New American menu with French, Italian, and heavy New Orleans touches (which is where he grew up). Look for oysters with green tomato vinaigrette, Louisiana crab claws in Cajun butter, steak with Swiss chard and turnips, and profiteroles with husk cherries.

Lobster roll pop-up Sailor & Siren opened as a full-on restaurant in early July in Greenpoint. Look for Maine lobster rolls with optional caviar and/or uni, as well as hot dogs sourced from Prospect Butcher Co., dressed with yes, caviar, or blueberry mustard. Desserts are simpler — whoopie pies and pocket pies.

The hit-making team behind Taqueria Ramirez and Carnitas Ramirez — chef Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar — opened their new soccer bar in Greenpoint in late May. After a busy World Cup season, the bar is slinging beers, tacos, and that Ramirez burger.

Is New York undergoing a Japanese pizza influx? The latest comes from a Vietnam-based international pizza chain that opened its first American location over Fourth of July weekend in Greenpoint. Pizza 4P’s (say it out loud) serves up Japanese Italian dishes and Neapolitan pies with global touches; see: spaghetti with oysters and seaweed, burrata ice cream, and pizza with lotus roots, pork sausage, and hummus or scallops and sweet miso gratin.

Two Texas barbecue superstars teamed up to open a dual-smoked meats joint right in Brooklyn this late August. Barbs B Q’s Chuck Charnichart and Goldee’s Jonny White opened Kirbee’s in Greenpoint, serving plates showcasing their specific points of view when it comes to barbecue. Charnichart takes on a South Texas-meets-Mexican angle with spiced brisket, pork ribs with lime zest, and green spaghetti; White’s approach is more modern, with classic brisket, smoked turkey, and potato salad. Per the way Texas barbecues, Kirbee’s is a casual lunchtime spot, with window ordering and a minimal indoor dining space.

Balera is Williamsburg’s newest pizzeria with two floors, a disco ball, and a menu rooted in the Italian regions of Piedmont and Emilia-Romagna, which opened in April. Look for thin-crust Roman-style pizza, pastas, and a seafood salad chock-full of octopus, shrimp, and potatoes. Per the name, which is Italian for “dance halls,” it’ll have live music or DJs on Friday and Saturday evenings.

While Llama Inn closed in 2025, the team decided to turn the modern Peruvian restaurant into a more casual South American-leaning tavern, which opened in May. Restaurateur Juan Correa and chef Francisco Castillo (their first initials make up the abbreviations in the restaurant name) are now showcasing South American cuisines more broadly, with Peruvian, Chilean, and Argentinian dishes, ingredients, and flavors. Grilled swordfish is served with yellow-eyed beans, and the arroz meloso is very lobster-laden. Drinks include wines from the regions and a special pisco sour.

Chef Jackie Carnesi is leading the kitchen of this breezy raw seafood bar in Williamsburg, which opened in May. Sibling to next-door Cafe Susanne, Bar Susanne serves New York and Northeast-sourced seafood, such as littleneck clam aguachile with passionfruit and hibiscus, pan-cooked whole fish, and brunch service, all in an elegant space with views of the East River and the Williamsburg Bridge.

Top Chef alum Rasika Venkatesa started Mythily, named after her grandmother, as a pop-up that explores Tamil and South Indian cuisines. And now she’s turned it into a restaurant in Williamsburg in September, with a color palette stemming from Kanchipuram saris. Food-wise, look for a scallop crudo with Concord grapes and puli inji, a pickled tamarind-ginger-green chile condiment, and finished with a granita made of jaggery, ginger, and warming spices; Caraflex cabbage that’s slow-roasted with spices and rebuilt layer by layer with sorrel-coconut chutney; and her popular rasmalai-tres leches dessert.

Chef Sirichai Sreparplarn revived his cult-favorite Thai restaurant after a 20-month shutter in Carroll Gardens, relocating to Williamsburg this late August. Ugly Baby 2.0 is now much larger, spread across two floors, with a full liquor license. This means much more room to enjoy his spicy Thai fare, plus cocktails, along with wine and a thoughtful beer list.

Zoli, the new “non-dogmatic seafood restaurant” from Houseman chef Ned Baldwin, is a partnership with Amant founder Lonti Ebers — a Houseman regular who named it after her imaginary dog. In April, GRT Architects converted a former warehouse into a huge space with a restaurant, bar, private dining room, and beautiful rooftop terrace. Anchoring the room is a commission by artist Pierre Huyghe featuring three large choreographed aquariums. On the menu: marinated mussels, surf clams with avocado and serrano peppers, and red shrimp tartare with husk cherries. Also try the bison strip steak or smoked goat sausage.

Pitmaster Ruben Santana first had his popular Queens pop-up, which turned into a Dumbo food hall stand, and has now transformed into its final form, a full restaurant in Bushwick, which opened in July. Bark Barbecue is centered on Central Texas barbecue with Dominican touches, which translates into carnitas fritas made with smoked and confited brisket trimmings placed on top of a fried plantain. There are classics, too, from smoked brisket to chicharrónes. The big indoor-outdoor space serves drinks now and includes a daytime coffee shop with breakfast tacos to come later.

It makes sense that Brooklyn Heights’ New American restaurant Confidant expanded next door with a new pizzeria, Frenzie, in August: Co-owners Daniel Grossman and Brendan Kelley worked at Roberta’s. On deck: New York-style pizza, natural wines by the glass and bottle, cocktails, and fun shots.

What’s old is new again in Cobble Hill: Sam’s has been around for quite some time, run by generations of the same family since 1930, but now by Georgia Fulton – a longtime server at the neighboring Long Island Bar who took the reins from previous owner Louis Migliaccio as of September. The Italian restaurant feels and looks wonderfully the same while tasting great, with slight updates like bar stools, the back dining room, and a slimmer menu, per Grub Street. There are still familiar dishes like the pizza and baked clams, alongside new ones like Caesar salads and pork chop Milanese.

The couple behind Grimm Artisanal Ales in Williamsburg expanded with the latest addition to the ongoing tavern trend in Prospect Heights in June, taking over the former Olmsted restaurant space. At Grimm Tavern, chef Greg Massaro (who had been at Dinosaur Bar-B-Que) is dishing out muffulettas, smash burgers, and roast chicken, alongside Grimm beers and Physica wines.

The team behind some of NYC’s hit seafood spots like Cervo’s opened a new oyster bar in Crown Heights this July. Zig Zag features raw-bar items sourced from Northeast waterways, including oysters, clams, and mussels, alongside peel-and-eat shrimp. Also look for lots of vegetables. It’s a walk-in spot meant to entice regulars for dinner.

Long live this new era of NYC taverns: The latest entrant comes from the team behind relocated Jewish deli Gertie’s and Jewish bistro Gertude’s, which opened in June. Trudie’s Tavern introduces rotisserie chicken, burgers, huge schnitzels, and bananas Foster sundaes from chefs Mike Cain and Eli Friedman.

More in Dining Out in NY

items.title: Where to Find the World’s Best Soup
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: 20,000 BC was a monumental year in history. Why? The first pot of soup was crafted in a cave in modern-day China. To create their savory broth, prehistoric
items.text:
20,000 BC was a monumental year in history. Why? The first pot of soup was crafted in a cave in modern-day China. To create their savory broth, prehistoric humans boiled animal bones and entrails in crude pits, then slurped their handiwork from some of the world’s earliest ceramic bowls.


Fast forward a few thousand years, and a verdict has been reached: Our ancient ancestors were onto something ... something delicious. Since this first boiling pot, humans have come up with all kinds of ways to make delicious, simmering broths, loading them full of tender meat, starches, vegetables, and herbs. From light and clear dishes with delicate flavors to chunky creations of the stew variety, there’s no wrong way to make or enjoy a bowl of soup. Just put a pot on the stove and let the spirit move you.


In honor of this most versatile and reliable of comfort foods, we’ve compiled our favorite places around the world to dig into a big bowl of soup. From a Russian restaurant hidden in a bathhouse to a New Orleans mainstay that fed the civil rights movement, these restaurants show that soup is universal—a dish that bridges divides and soothes the soul. Grab your biggest spoon and your bib (because, yes, there will be spillage); we’re going on a delicious journey.


1. Wattana Panich - Bangkok, Thailand


Can soup be eternal? Apparently so, as this Bangkok eatery has been tending to the same massive, boiling pot of neua tune (beef stew) for 50 years. Owner Nattapong Kaweenuntawong has cooked this famous “half-century-old soup” since he was a kid working under his father, keeping the secret blend of spices and herbs, stewed beef, raw beef slices, meatballs, tripe, and other organs perfectly balanced. The ancient practice Kaweenuntawong uses to keep the soup constantly simmering is called Hunter’s Stew, using the previous day’s leftover broth as the base of the following day’s soup.


The process is time-consuming and quite labor-intensive, with Kaweenuntawong tearing through about 150 pounds of beef each day and cooking the meat until it is tender (about 11 hours in total). It’s well-worth the effort, though, for the rich, flavorful creation that emerges, with melt-in-your-mouth meat, chewy noodles, and an irresistible aroma.

2. Bún Riêu Gánh - Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


If you’re out shopping in Ben Thanh Market, you might just stumble across a huge pot of crab broth hanging from a wooden yoke, or gánh, and loaded with rice vermicelli noodles and a special crab meatloaf made with crab paste, minced pork, and egg. This would be Bún Riêu Gánh, the passion project of local legend Mrs. Mai Thi Lien. For four decades, she’s been ladling out generous portions of this traditional noodle soup to hungry passersby, with dipping cups of tamarind fish sauce and chili that lend the dish a tangy, southern-Vietnamese twist.

3. Matryoshka at Wall Street Bath & Spa 88 - New York, New York


On a small street tucked away between skyscrapers in the Financial District, this subterranean bath and spa has a few tricks up its sleeve (of the comfort food variety). After making your way through a labyrinth of stairwells and passageways (where you may pass more than a few toweled patrons), you’ll end up in a quaint bar/restaurant decorated with intricate wood carvings and Russian nesting dolls, matryoshkas, that the restaurant gets it name from.


Here, still in your robe and slippers, you can enjoy some of the best Eastern European food in the Big Apple, like buzhenina, an herb-roasted pork tenderloin from Russia and Ukraine, or a Georgian lamb soup known as harcho. Soup seekers can also find borsch, fish soup, and chicken soup with dumplings, as well as solyanka, a meaty Russian soup with green olives and briny pickles. Make your visit even more special with a glass of infused vodka or a pint of Russian lager, then sweat it all out in the sauna.

4. Fio D’Italia - San Francisco, California


Established in 1886 in San Francisco’s North Beach neighborhood, Fio D’Italia holds the title of “America’s Oldest Italian Restaurant” and still serves up dishes from its early days such as scaloppine fior, tender veal sautéed with prosciutto and mushrooms in wine sauce; petto di pollo alla Valdosta, chicken breast cooked with prosciutto and fontina cheese; and, last but not least, a classic minestrone soup loaded with winter beans and vegetables.

Also on the menu is a zuppa di cavolo con formaggio, a cabbage, bread and cheese stew with bits of prosciutto; and pasta e fagioli, a soup with—you guessed it—pasta, cannellini beans, and prosciutto. You can also rest assured that a thick, crusty half loaf of sourdough French bread will be brought to your table, complete with flaky salt and extra virgin olive oil. Mamma mia!

5. Au Pied de Cochon - Paris, France


Au Pied de Cochon was once known for using all parts of the pig in its dishes, from marrow bones to kidneys to heads and the eponymous hooves (it was founded by a former butcher after all). These days, however, people more often come for its soupe à l’oignon au gratin, or French onion soup—a decadent dish full of caramelized onions, gooey cheese, and baguette slices.

Unlike most other versions of French onion soup, which use beef stock as a base, Au Pied’s uses chicken stock to honor its Les Halles roots. Back when the area was still Paris’s central fresh food market, the soup became a go-to meal for blue collar workers and night owls roaming the “belly of Paris.” And since Au Pied de Cochon is open almost 24 hours a day (8 a.m. to 5 a.m.), you can still eat this fine soup at almost all hours of the night. (It’s perhaps even more delicious after an evening out.)


6. Chankonabe Shinzan - Tokyo, Japan

This tiny, hole-in-the-wall shop serves up a mean bowl of chanko nabe, a soup that combines meat or fish with tofu, vegetables, glutinous rice, and broth. The dish has long been the favorite of sumo wrestlers for bulking up and fueling for a fight, and Chankonabe Shinzan was, in fact, founded by Shinzan Takeyasu, a retired sumo wrestler and soup-maker extraordinaire.

Shinzan’s restaurant serves chanko nabe with both salt and curry-based broths (though the curry varieties are the clear favorite among locals). If you need something to tide you over till your soup is ready, there are appetizers like wagyu beef topped with green onions, snow crab salad, and tebasaki, double-fried chicken wings in a sweet-savory soy glaze. Just make sure to save room for the main event!

7. Appu’s Cafe - Long Beach, California


The rich soups at this Indian-Mexican fusion cafe are just what the doctor ordered ... literally. Appu’s was opened by Dr. Vinod Venkataraman in his retirement after a long career spent extolling the virtues of gingery broths and lentil stews. Chef VR (as those in the know call him) abides by the mantra: “Healthy eating is a choice, eating healthy is a lifestyle,” meaning everything on Appu’s menu is nutrient-dense and guilt-free.

Whether you opt for the spicy, protein-filled garbanzo bean soup or the creamy, nutty spinach soup, you’re in for a flavor-packed, warm, and satisfying treat. Pro tip: Pair your soup with the Maharani burrito, filled with rice pilaf and lentils and served with a special secret sauce.


8. A Touch of European Cafe - Glendale, Arizona


This family-owned joint serves up “pure comfort food done right”: hearty Polish classics like goulash, kielbasa, stuffed cabbage, and—to top it all off—an extensive list of signature soups. There’s truly a soup for everyone here, with options ranging from New England clam chowder to potato horseradish to chilled garlic; cold buttermilk and beets to cream of asparagus and beef tripe. All of these signatures pair perfectly with the cafe’s dark rye bread and pierogis, which you can wash down with a caramel apple cider or iced tea.


You can even learn how to make A Touch of European’s soups yourself at one of their twice-annual cooking classes, led by chef and owner Waldemar Okul. Whether you grew up on Polish cuisine or know only the basics, you’ll walk away from the experience with a Rolodex of beloved recipes to make at home. Past classes have included dishes like caprese on apricot walnut bread, chilled avocado and dill soup and, for dessert, a puff pastry Napoleon.

9. Dooky Chase’s Restaurant - New Orleans, Louisiana


Established in 1939, this NOLA institution has fed everyone from President Barack Obama to Nat King Cole and Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. Though Edgar “Dooky” and Emily Chase first opened Dooky’s as a sandwich shop, it grew into an upscale celebration of Creole cuisine after Leah, the Chases’ daughter-in-law, took over the business in the ’50s. As part of this revamp, she featured work by local Black artists on the restaurants’ walls—the first time many of them had seen their works publicly displayed.


Leah also added regional favorites like shrimp clemenceau, chicken creole, and creole gumbo to Dooky Chase’s menu, the latter of which still draws crowds with its winning combination of crab, shrimp, veal, and smoked and hot sausage. The restaurant also serves its signature green gumbo in the days leading up to Easter (made with nine different cooked greens). It may not look especially delicious, but it sure does taste good.


10. Farren’s Bar - Malin Head, Ireland


Ireland’s northernmost pub has been in the Farren family for six generations, drawing in folks from across County Donegal with its delicious seafood chowder and buttery, homemade soda bread. It’s the perfect hearty meal after a hike along Malin Head’s rocky cliffs or a swim through the harbor (especially if you add a Guinness to your order). The pub also boasts a fun bit of “Star Wars” trivia, having been visited by Mark Hamill during the filming of “The Last Jedi,” and even has a Yoda mural on its exterior.

11. Caldo de Piedra - Tlalixtac de Cabrera, Mexico


This small outpost outside Oaxaca is named after its signature dish, a fish and shrimp soup that is a staple of the indigenous Chinantec community. Traditionally, men would cook the soup right on the riverbank, seasoning their freshly caught fish with onions, lime, cilantro, and chiles. Caldo de Piedra keeps this centuries-old tradition alive today, using the same kind of fire-heated rocks to flash-cook and tenderize the fish. In fact, so revered is this practice that owner César Gachupín had to seek permission from town elders before opening his restaurant.


In 2021, the state’s congress declared the dish an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Oaxaca for its “symbolic importance as one of the dishes that best reflects the culture and society of the Papaloapan region.” Though it has historically been made by men, the soup is seen as a gesture of gratitude toward the women, children, and elders of the community.


12. Rung Rueang - Bangkok, Thailand


The tom yum soup at this unassuming spot has gained a cult following amongst Bangkok foodies, with large chunks of spicy-sweet pork balanced out by hints of lemongrass, chile, and lime. While this is the standard version of the dish, Rung Rueang offers plenty of ways to customize, with different broth bases, noodle types, and toppings: sugar if you wish to temper the heat, or a dusting of chile flakes to crank it up. The soup is so life-altering that Rung Rueang has been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand designation every year since 2018 and often has a line that snakes down the block.


Arriving to the shop, you’ll notice that it is, in fact, divided into two sections—the result of a decades-long family feud. While both still serve the dishes under the same names, the “left-side” shop (the original) is widely considered the better of the two.

11. Caldo de Piedra - Tlalixtac de Cabrera, Mexico

This small outpost outside Oaxaca is named after its signature dish, a fish and shrimp soup that is a staple of the indigenous Chinantec community. Traditionally, men would cook the soup right on the riverbank, seasoning their freshly caught fish with onions, lime, cilantro, and chiles. Caldo de Piedra keeps this centuries-old tradition alive today, using the same kind of fire-heated rocks to flash-cook and tenderize the fish. In fact, so revered is this practice that owner César Gachupín had to seek permission from town elders before opening his restaurant.

In 2021, the state’s congress declared the dish an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Oaxaca for its “symbolic importance as one of the dishes that best reflects the culture and society of the Papaloapan region.” Though it has historically been made by men, the soup is seen as a gesture of gratitude toward the women, children, and elders of the community.
12. Rung Rueang - Bangkok, Thailand

The tom yum soup at this unassuming spot has gained a cult following amongst Bangkok foodies, with large chunks of spicy-sweet pork balanced out by hints of lemongrass, chile, and lime. While this is the standard version of the dish, Rung Rueang offers plenty of ways to customize, with different broth bases, noodle types, and toppings: sugar if you wish to temper the heat, or a dusting of chile flakes to crank it up. The soup is so life-altering that Rung Rueang has been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand designation every year since 2018 and often has a line that snakes down the block.

Arriving to the shop, you’ll notice that it is, in fact, divided into two sections—the result of a decades-long family feud. While both still serve the dishes under the same names, the “left-side” shop (the original) is widely considered the better of the two.
